finds.name: Valeriana
finds.label: Valeriana
finds.period: Classic Maya city; at its peak around 750–850 CE
finds.survey: Lidar flown in 2013 to measure forest carbon; re-read for archaeology by Luke Auld-Thomas (Tulane) and colleagues
finds.description: A Classic Maya city with two monumental centres about 2 km apart, linked by dense houses, causeways and terraces, spread over 16.6 km². It sits about 15 minutes' walk from the region's only highway, among fields farmed for years, yet no archaeologist had recorded it. The same survey counted 6,674 previously unknown structures.
finds.changed: Major Maya cities are still missing from the map. Even a capital-sized site next to a highway was unknown until 2024, so empty-looking jungle on older maps usually means unsurveyed, not unsettled.

confidence.reason: The city is certain; the pin is placed near Xpujil to about 10 km, because the published maps do not give exact coordinates.

sources.title: Auld-Thomas et al. 2024, Running out of empty space (Antiquity)
BBC News: Lost Mayan city found in Mexico jungle by accident

finds.name: Maya lowlands lidar (PACUNAM)
finds.label: 61,480 Maya structures
finds.period: Mostly Late Classic Maya, about 600–900 CE
finds.survey: PACUNAM Lidar Initiative, flown 2016 over 2,144 km² of the Maya Biosphere Reserve
finds.description: The largest lidar survey of the Maya world at the time mapped 61,480 ancient structures, about 29 per km², along with causeways, reservoirs, terraced and drained fields, and defensive walls and moats linking cities like Tikal to their countryside.
finds.changed: It turned scattered temple cities into one continuous, engineered landscape. The authors estimate that 7–11 million people lived in the central Maya lowlands in the Late Classic.

confidence.reason: Peer-reviewed survey with published maps; the pin marks the centre of the survey area (Tikal), which covers about 50 km around it.

sources.title: Canuto et al. 2018, Ancient lowland Maya complexity (Science)

finds.name: Mirador–Calakmul causeways
finds.label: Mirador causeways
finds.period: Middle and Late Preclassic Maya, about 1000 BCE – 150 CE
finds.survey: Airborne lidar of the Mirador–Calakmul Karst Basin (flown 2015), analysed by Richard Hansen and colleagues
finds.description: Lidar mapped 964 settlements in and around the basin, grouped into 417 cities, towns and villages, joined by more than 177 km of raised causeways. Platforms and pyramids at El Mirador are among the largest ever built by the Maya.
finds.changed: Large, planned and connected Maya cities existed centuries before the Classic period, and the authors argue they point to organised, state-like rule in the Preclassic.

confidence.reason: The settlements and causeways are mapped; how centralised the early network was is still debated.

sources.title: Hansen et al. 2022, LiDAR analyses in the Mirador–Calakmul Karst Basin (Ancient Mesoamerica)
Reuters: Ancient Maya cities, 'super highways' revealed

finds.name: Aguada Fénix
finds.label: Aguada Fénix
finds.survey: Low-resolution government lidar, then targeted high-resolution lidar and excavation by Takeshi Inomata and colleagues
finds.description: A raised earthen platform 1,400 m long and 10–15 m high, with nine causeways leading off it. It is the oldest and largest monumental structure known in the Maya area, and it is so long and low that on the ground it looks like natural landscape.
finds.changed: The site shows few signs of a ruling elite, which suggests early communities could build huge monuments before strong kings appeared.

confidence.reason: Dated by excavation and radiocarbon; the site's location is published.

sources.title: Inomata et al. 2020, Monumental architecture at Aguada Fénix (Nature)

finds.name: Angamuco
finds.label: Angamuco
finds.period: Purépecha (Tarascan) city, founded around 900 CE, peak about 1000–1350 CE
finds.survey: Airborne lidar of a rugged lava field, analysed by Christopher Fisher (Colorado State) and colleagues
finds.description: Lidar of a jagged lava flow revealed a city of more than 40,000 building foundations over about 26 km²: houses, pyramids, plazas, ball courts, terraces and a network of roads, possibly home to over 100,000 people at its peak.
finds.changed: Fisher thinks it was the most populous city in western Mexico in its time, bigger in area than the later Purépecha capital Tzintzuntzan, and it showed that lidar finds cities on bare rock as well as under forest.

confidence.reason: The foundations are mapped; the population figure is the project's estimate.

sources.title: The Guardian: Laser scanning reveals 'lost' ancient Mexican city
Fisher et al. 2019, A typology of ancient Purépecha architecture from Angamuco (Latin American Antiquity)

finds.name: Greater Angkor's hidden city
finds.label: Angkor's hidden grid
finds.period: Khmer capital region, about 9th–15th centuries CE
finds.survey: Khmer Archaeology LiDAR Consortium, flown 2012 (Damian Evans and colleagues); extended by the Cambodian Archaeological Lidar Initiative in 2015
finds.description: Under the forest around Angkor Wat, lidar revealed a formally planned urban grid of roads, ponds, house mounds and embankments that the great temples were set into, plus huge water-management works across the plain.
finds.changed: Angkor was not a temple complex in empty forest but the core of the largest low-density city of the pre-industrial world, and the strain on its waterworks helps explain its decline.

confidence.reason: Peer-reviewed survey; the pin marks Angkor Wat at the centre of the mapped city.

sources.title: Evans et al. 2013, Uncovering archaeological landscapes at Angkor using lidar (PNAS)

finds.name: Mahendraparvata
finds.label: Mahendraparvata
finds.survey: The same 2012 Angkor lidar campaign, followed by the 2015 survey and fieldwork (published in Antiquity, 2019)
finds.description: A city on the Phnom Kulen plateau known mainly from inscriptions, where Jayavarman II was proclaimed king in 802. Lidar showed a planned grid with a palace, a state temple, dams and a reservoir, hidden under forest.
finds.changed: It confirmed that the first Khmer imperial capital was a real planned city, built before the move down to the Angkor plain.

confidence.reason: Mapped by lidar and checked by excavation; the pin sits on the plateau city.

sources.title: Chevance et al. 2019, Mahendraparvata: an early Angkor-period capital (Antiquity)

finds.name: Upano valley garden cities
finds.label: Upano garden cities
finds.period: About 500 BCE to 300–600 CE (Kilamope and Upano cultures)
finds.survey: Lidar flown in 2015 for Ecuador's National Institute of Cultural Heritage, analysed with decades of excavation by Stéphen Rostain and colleagues
finds.description: Lidar mapped clusters of earthen platforms around plazas, joined by wide, straight roads running for tens of kilometres, with drained fields and terraces between them, on the eastern foot of the Andes.
finds.changed: It is the oldest known urban network in the Amazon, about a thousand years older than other known examples, which overturns the idea that the rainforest could not support cities.

confidence.reason: The landscape is mapped, but the start and end dates rest on few radiocarbon samples and have been challenged.

sources.title: Rostain et al. 2024, Two thousand years of garden urbanism in the Upper Amazon (Science)
CNRS News: Ancient cities in the Amazon

finds.name: Cotoca and Landívar (Casarabe culture)
finds.label: Casarabe towns
finds.survey: Airborne lidar analysed by Heiko Prümers (German Archaeological Institute) and colleagues
finds.description: Two large settlements, Cotoca (147 ha) and Landívar (315 ha), with stepped platforms, U-shaped structures and conical pyramids up to 22 m tall, ringed by banks and joined to smaller sites by straight raised causeways several kilometres long, with canals and reservoirs.
finds.changed: It was the first clear evidence of low-density urbanism in pre-Hispanic Amazonia, like that known from the Maya and Angkor.

confidence.reason: The sites are mapped and dated; the pin is placed in the Casarabe area to about 20 km.

sources.title: Prümers et al. 2022, Lidar reveals pre-Hispanic low-density urbanism in the Bolivian Amazon (Nature)

finds.name: Tugunbulak and Tashbulak
finds.label: Tugunbulak
finds.period: Medieval highland towns, 6th to late 10th century CE
finds.survey: Drone lidar in 2022 by Michael Frachetti (Washington University in St. Louis), Farhod Maksudov and colleagues
finds.description: At 2,000–2,200 m, drone lidar traced walls, fortifications, terraces and a citadel spread over about 120 ha at Tugunbulak, with the smaller Tashbulak 5 km away. They were centres of iron mining and working on the mountain routes of the Silk Roads.
finds.changed: It showed that big medieval towns, not just nomad camps, stood high in Central Asia's mountains on the Silk Roads.

confidence.reason: Mapped by lidar and excavation; site coordinates are published.

sources.title: Frachetti et al. 2024, Large-scale medieval urbanism traced by UAV–lidar in highland Central Asia (Nature)
